_comment: The redaction rules FR-012 is judged against (spec 037, research R6,
contracts/attachments.md §2).
One list, two consumers: apps/web/src/services/feedbackRedaction.ts
applies it in the browser at push time into the log ring buffer, and the
server's feedback validator applies the same list to the approved payload
and *refuses* rather than rewrites. A rule that existed only on the server
would produce refusals the person could not have anticipated; a rule that
existed only on the client would be no rule at all. So neither side owns
the rules — this file does.
It lives in config/ next to realm-defaults.json and is read the same way:
imported by the bundler on the web side, include_str! on the Rust side.
A rule set that can be absent at runtime is a rule set that will be.
PATTERN DIALECT — the one constraint that matters. Every pattern here
must mean the same thing to JavaScript's RegExp and to Rust's `regex`
crate, so it is written in the subset both share: no lookahead, no
lookbehind, no backreferences (Rust has none of them), and no inline
flags (each side sets them from `ignore_case`). Matching is always
global — every occurrence in a line, not the first. Replacements are
literal text with no capture-group references, because `$1` and `${1}`
do not mean the same thing on both sides.
Every replacement is VISIBLE. A secret is never silently deleted: the
person is entitled to see that something was removed and what kind of
thing it was, and a silent removal is indistinguishable from a rule that
never fired.
Order is significant. Rules are applied in the order listed, so the
widest shapes (a PEM block, a whole header line) come before the narrow
ones that could otherwise chew a hole in the middle of them.
A rule marked "dynamic": true has no pattern here because its pattern is
not a constant — it is built at runtime from a value the side in question
knows (the signed-in account's own email address). It is declared anyway
so that both sides agree the kind exists and share its replacement.

rules.why: A private key pasted or logged in full. Widest shape, so it runs first: the base64 body would otherwise be diced up by the jwt and aws_key rules and the result would still contain most of the key. The second alternative takes everything after a BEGIN marker that has no END — a key truncated by the per-entry byte bound is still a key, and both engines prefer the leftmost alternative, so a complete block still ends at its END line.

Cookie and Set-Cookie headers, and the session cookie's own name wherever it appears in an assignment. The names are the two this product actually sets: crates/thunderforge-axum-auth-core/src/session.rs SESSION_COOKIE_NAME and CSRF_COOKIE_NAME. Matching the bare word `session` anywhere would redact half of every log this feature exists to deliver, so it is matched only where it is being assigned a value.
An Authorization header, or a bare `Bearer <token>` in a logged request. The header prefix is optional so that a token logged on its own is still caught.

A compact JWS triple. Two alternatives rather than a generic xxx.yyy.zzz, which would redact every dotted package name and hostname in the buffer: the first anchors on `eyJ` (the base64url of `{"`, which every JWT header begins with), the second catches a non-JWT dotted token only when all three segments are long enough that no ordinary identifier could be mistaken for one.

How a presigned storage URL leaks. Not hypothetical: src/server/src/storage/rustfs.rs mints per-call STS credentials scoped to one key, and a failing asset fetch logs the URL that carried them. The leading ? or & is consumed because Rust's regex has no lookbehind, so the separator cannot be matched without being taken.
Access key ids have a fixed shape; STS session tokens have a recognisable prefix; a secret access key has no shape at all, so it is caught by the name it is written down under.

FR-013: the submitter's address must not reach the destination, and a log line is one of the two routes it could take (the other is the issue body, which carries an opaque submission reference instead). Dynamic because the address is not a constant — the client learns it from the signed-in account, the server from the row.
